title: Gratitude
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up gratitude after setting aside his planned talk on the paramitas, and describes a personal experiment sparked by a quote at the Y: "Any amount of gratitude changes the present." When his mind drifts toward complaint, Seishu stops and asks what he can genuinely feel grateful for. In a noisy tent camp at Yosemite, he thinks of people who lost their homes in the Nepal earthquake and lets the irritation go. Seishu draws on Brother David Steindl-Rast, Dogen's Fukanzazengi, and Norman Fischer, and closes by reading Norman's One Heart Grace before inviting everyone to name something they are grateful for.

sentences.text: Well, good evening everybody and welcome.
Glad to see everyone here.
Now, when I volunteered to give this talk a couple of months ago, I was planning to talk on the paramitas: wisdom, patience, generosity, ethical conduct, meditation, and effort.
They're so straightforward, unlike a lot of things in Zen and Buddhism.
I really like them and I try to keep them in mind and incorporate them in my day-to-day life.

I even bought a book on the paramitas, which I was going to read in preparation for this talk, but I guess that means I'll be giving another talk later, because I decided I actually wanted to talk about something different tonight, and that is gratitude.
So the paramitas will have to wait for another time.
It wasn't anything in particular that got me interested in gratitude, but I just kept running into it in unexpected ways.
I'd be reading an article about something else and gratitude would come up, or I'd be having conversations with people and the subject of gratitude would come up.
About a month ago I was at the Y, and they post quotes in the lobby, and there was a really good one on gratitude.
I don't recall who said it, but the quote was, "No amount of regret changes the past.
No amount of anxiety changes the future.
Any amount of gratitude changes the present."
That really stuck with me.
So I thought, I'm going to experiment.
I want to see if that is actually true.
I thought I would try to work more with gratitude in my day-to-day life.
The way I did that: I don't know about anybody else's mind, but if I just let my mind drift and not pay attention to what I'm thinking about, every so often I'll go to the negative.
I'll find myself making a list of all the things that aren't the way I want them to be.
Often they're little things.

I don't like the weather today, or somebody just drove by and they're going too fast or they're making noise, or I bought something recently and it was too expensive or it wasn't as good as I thought it would be.
Then if I happen to go from there to politics or to the big problems in the world, poverty, war, natural disasters, I can find myself in a really negative place.
Really negative.
So I thought, what I'll try to do is just catch myself, and regular meditation really helps with that.
You can really catch your mind going in a direction that isn't going to do you any good.
So I would just say stop, and then I would ask myself, right now, is there anything that I genuinely can feel grateful about?
I was surprised that every time I asked that question, things would just pop up.
I'm grateful for my health, I'm grateful to be married to my wife Carolyn, grateful that my daughter moved back to Seattle from the East Coast, et cetera, et cetera.
Sometimes the same things would come up.
I love living in Bellingham, but always something.
So that was really great.
It really seemed like that quote, that any amount of gratitude changes the present, is true, because it really improved my mood.
I can give one more example of how that little experiment worked.
A couple of weeks ago, I was in Yosemite with a friend and we were hiking for five days.
I'd never been to Yosemite.
It's a stunning place, with amazing geology, huge rock walls, beautiful meadows, forests and a couple of rivers running through it.
All the waterfalls were full and it was incredible.
But it is really crowded.
I don't know how many people are in Yosemite on any given day, but thousands for sure.
We stayed in a place called Curry Village, which is basically a tent camp.
You can rent a tent with cots in it for the night, and the tents are five feet apart and there are hundreds of them.
So it was really noisy at night, even though they have signs up that say quiet after 10 p.m.
It was not quiet after 10 p.m.

You could hear conversations all over the place, and people would be coming in late at night, having just arrived at Yosemite, saying, "Where's my tent?" and dragging their suitcases across the gravel.
The first night I was just getting steamed.
Luckily I caught myself and I realized that if I keep thinking this way, I'm really going to have a miserable night.
So I was able to stop and say, okay, this cot is comfortable.
I'm warm.
The tent's okay.
I'm in a really beautiful place.
I'm only going to be here for four or five days, so if I don't get that much sleep at night, that's okay.

Then I thought about all the people in the world who don't even have a tent, the people in Nepal who lost their homes to the earthquake, people in refugee camps who may be living there for years with no future.
They don't know when they're going to get out of there, or if they ever will.
That kind of thinking cut that negative dialogue right off, and it was very helpful.
So that's another good example of how gratitude can make a difference in your day-to-day, moment-to-moment life.
I realized that I'm giving examples of what I would call trivial problems.
If you don't like the weather or if somebody's making too much noise, it's really not that big a deal.
But I think a great deal of our lives is spent being irritated at trivial things, when you think about it and when you look back on it.
So it's very helpful to be able to just cut that off and to feel better.
I'm planning to continue doing my research on gratitude by doing this day-to-day stuff.

I do want to make sure and mention that I'm not suggesting that we use gratitude to turn a blind eye to the big problems in the world or to any big personal problems that all of us are going to have from time to time.
I think it's really important to notice a problem, to feel it, to acknowledge it, and then, by thinking about it, to take some action that might make things better.
Paying that kind of attention to problems is really important.
But because of the little experiments I've done on gratitude, the world just feels like a more generous place.
That's a good feeling to carry around.
I'd also like to share a couple of things that I came across in my reading and research on gratitude.
First of all, if you Google gratitude, there are dozens and dozens and dozens of websites devoted to gratitude.
I'm not much of a computer guy, so I was pretty surprised by this.
There are many websites that just have gratitude quotes.
There are websites that talk about how to be more grateful.
There are websites that do scientific research on gratitude.
And did you know that according to one of these websites, if you feel more gratitude, you will be more successful?
One article talked about gratitude being an emotional muscle that will grow and develop if you use it intentionally.
There's even an app for gratitude.

With this app, you list five things every day that you feel grateful about and you keep them in mind during the day, and according to this little article, if you do that for 21 days, you can rewire your brain.
I chuckled at that, but then I realized that's what I was trying to do with my experiment of interrupting my negative thinking.
So anyway, the topic has become very popular and mainstream, and there's a lot out there on it.
One person I discovered in my reading is a man named Brother David Steindl Rast.
He's a Benedictine monk, and he's been studying and working with gratitude for decades.
I think he's in his early 80s now.
He's a friend of Norman Fischer.
Norman, for those of you who don't know, lives in California, and he's the guiding teacher of the sangha.
He comes up here a couple of times a year, and he's been involved with us for many, many years.
Brother David talks about how people want to feel joy.
They don't really want things and stuff, but often they're going after things and stuff in order to feel better.
But gratitude brings much more joy than any possession.
He also talks about how important it is to slow down.
If you're moving through life too quickly, you just can't see all the things that are out there that you might end up feeling glad about.
So it's important to slow down.

And I think all of us could list people who have helped us along the way, people that we feel grateful to, whether it's been emotional support or practical things like helping with education or helping with living expenses.
But several writers talked about paying attention to things that are given to us for free, that we just get because we're alive.
One of those things, of course, is your life.
Not one of us in this room asked to be alive, asked to be born, but here we are.
We all have a human life.
In Buddhist writing, we didn't do anything to earn this life, but here we are.
In many places in Buddhist writing, it's mentioned how rare it is to be born into a human life.
In Fukanzazengi, Eihei Dogen, the 12th century Japanese priest that we study a lot around here, writes,
*You have gained the pivotal opportunity of human form.
Do not use your time in vain.*
Another thing that's freely given is the beauty of nature.
Every sunrise, every sunset, the clouds, the mountains, the trees, they're there every day for us to enjoy.
And here's something I hardly ever think about: how about spoken and written language?
Every one of us, of course, had people teach us how to write and how to read and how to speak, but it took human beings thousands of years to develop the ability to speak a language.
We come along at a time and we are the beneficiaries of that.
I hardly ever think about that, but that's really pretty amazing.
Then there are, of course, developments in medicine and technology and architecture, all the things that human beings have been improving over the years.
We come along in the 21st century and we just get these things for free.
And Zen practice is another example of that.

It's available to us today because of all the teachers and all the practitioners over the last 2,500 years who did this meditation practice and passed it on from person to person until we get to have it today.
In a talk on suffering and gratitude, Norman Fischer said,
*So we are all training, cultivating every day the sense of gratefulness, which is the happiest of all attitudes.
You cannot feel gratitude and unhappiness in the same moment.
If you feel grateful, you feel happy.
You feel grateful for what is possible for you in this moment, no matter what your challenges are.
You feel grateful that you are alive at all, grateful that you can think, that you can feel, stand up, sit down, walk, talk.
These are all miracles.*
One writer talked about the feeling of appreciation for what is as something that can be thought of as a natural expression of Buddha nature.

I found that paying more attention to gratitude makes me feel better moment by moment, but it also makes it less overwhelming to look at and try to respond to the big problems in the world, or the big problems that I have from time to time in my life.
The world feels more balanced.
And getting back to the paramitas, I definitely feel more patient and more generous because I've been paying attention to gratitude.
I feel like I'm more able to give my time and energy and resources to others.
So it's been a really excellent project to work on, and I highly recommend it to all of you: on a day-to-day basis, try to pay a little more attention to gratitude and see how that feels.
The last thing I want to do is finish by reciting a prayer that Norman Fischer wrote entitled One Heart Grace.
Some of you know this.
He wrote this to say before meals, and Carolyn and I often say this before meals.
Once when we were having dinner with Norman, we said the prayer and his comment afterward was, "It's kind of long."
But I don't think it is.
I really like it, and in just a few words it kind of summarizes what I've been talking about.
So I'll read it to you right now.
This is called One Heart Grace.

*As we make ready to eat this food, we remember with gratitude the many people, tools, animals and plants, air and water, sky and earth turned in the wheel of living and dying whose joyful exertion provide our sustenance this day.
May we, with the blessing of this food, join our hearts to the one heart of the world in awareness and love.
And may we, together with everyone, realize the path of awakening and never stop making effort for the benefit of others.*
Thank you very much for listening.
I knew this was going to be a short talk, so I thought what we could do.
Oh, it's not that short.
We have time for this.
We could actually go around one at a time, and if you wanted to say one or two things that you feel grateful about, just whatever spontaneously comes up.
You're also welcome to just pass if you don't want to say anything.
So why don't we do that?
Do you want to start out?
Very excited to be here for some more time.
I'm grateful for having the Sangha, this opportunity to practice so near home.
I'm grateful for having my best friend in town for one thing.
I'm grateful that my brother's coming home from China tomorrow.
Just living in Bellingham, that's one grateful aspect of my life.
I came across that quote from Norman Fischer a couple of nights ago about him saying, if you are grateful, you can't be unhappy.
And usually I just am not, as I'm reading.
And that just stopped me cold.
And it's absolutely right.
And I can see why a lot of groups all over the world use gratefulness as a cornerstone.
So it's much appreciated.
Thank you.
Good talk.
I've been really grateful for the sense of community recently, noticing how small and widespread your own personal community can be.
I'm grateful for my brother's invitation to invite me out to Washington in the first place, and then establishing Zen practice in my life after attending here for my first time about six weeks ago.
I'm grateful to live in the Pacific Northwest.
It's such a nice place to live all the time.
I'm grateful for the ideas and thoughts of strangers.

Gosh, I'm grateful for being out and breathing and [unclear: "from family, specializing in family"] and, actually, I was just thinking earlier, I'm grateful to have so many circles of colleagues and friends, more and more everywhere, in all different walks of life.
My kind of idea of what kind of person I'm allowed to be connected to has just washed away.
I'm more allowed to be connected to everybody regardless of their station in life or their background or anything.
So I'm grateful for that, the sense of connection.
I'm grateful to have people to rely on and to be with.
I'm grateful for this moment right here right now and everybody in this room who is sharing it.
I'm grateful for the time that I'm getting to spend with my first family, my sisters and my mother.
We're all helping her go through the process of dying right now, and there are so many things that come up that I'm so grateful for.
Just connecting with my sisters and my nieces and my mother, and I'm also very thankful for this time.

There's a theme of community this evening that people are grateful for, and that's what I'm grateful for, especially having people in my different activities telling me about things in another activity that we also hold in common.
So it's kind of like a Venn diagram.
Everything's in the mix and delights me.
This may sound pretty trivial compared to what a lot of people have said, but to me it's not.
I'm grateful for my dog.
With my back surgery he's a reason for me to get myself out of bed, because I've got to get him his breakfast.
This morning I took him for a walk.
Even though I didn't really feel like it, I took him out.
The sun was shining through the trees, and I walk slowly these days, so it's really looking at these woods and the sun coming through.
So I'm grateful for Angus.
I'm grateful for the timing of the talk on gratitude tonight, and it seems to keep happening every time I come here.
The Dharma talks are such good timing for me and my life.
I'm very grateful for that.
I'm grateful for the gratitude that I'm going to experience tomorrow.
I have a 12 year old son who's incredibly wise for his age, so I enjoy that and I'm grateful for that.
I'm grateful for a sense of humor, for the people around me who have a sense of humor.
I'm grateful for how wonderful my life is.
Parts that are fun, and I'm grateful for the parts that challenge me because they make me a better person.
I'm grateful for the Sangha and the community.
